p5c1.essay:
After four parts spent almost entirely inside Raskolnikov's fever, Dostoevsky opens Part Five by handing the book to the man it likes least. I find that a relief and a provocation at once. Luzhin at the looking-glass, checking himself for jaundice and consoled by his own ‘noble, clear-skinned countenance,’ is pure comedy, and the comedy has teeth. His one regret about [[p4c2|last night's rupture]] is that he did not spend fifteen hundred roubles on presents, because people like Dounia and her mother ‘would feel bound to return money and presents’ and would find it hard. Generosity, for him, is a way of putting people in his debt. I'd keep that in mind every time money changes hands in this chapter.

The long middle is the novel's broadest satire, and it helps to know what is being mocked. Lebeziatnikov is a parody of the young radicals of the 1860s who took their programme from Chernyshevsky's novel What Is to Be Done?: communes, free marriage, usefulness as the only measure of worth, cesspool-cleaning ranked above Raphael and Pushkin. The debate about whether a commune member may walk into another's room at any hour is Dostoevsky turning one of that novel's earnest domestic rules inside out. The narrator's own verdict is savage (‘half-animate abortions’) and I think it is the least fair sentence in the book so far, because what the scene shows is more interesting than the insult. Lebeziatnikov is absurd, but he is ‘rather soft-hearted,’ he blushes, he respects Sonia in his muddled way, and he believes what he says. Luzhin believes nothing. He picked up ‘current phrases’ before [[p2c5|his first call on Raskolnikov]] purely as insurance, and he sits clicking his abacus and sniggering while the younger man talks. One of them has silly ideas and a decent heart; the other has no ideas at all and a use for everybody. Dostoevsky loathes the ideas, but he is too honest a novelist to hide which of the two is worse company.

Then Sonia is fetched, and the temperature drops. She sits down three times, cannot find a safe place to rest her eyes, and agrees to the word ‘preternatural’ because she would agree to anything to get out of the room. Luzhin insists on a witness, asks in a whisper whether Raskolnikov has arrived next door, and holds out a ten-rouble note ‘carefully unfolded.’ I would watch his hands rather than listen to his sentences. The chapter ends with him rubbing them, and with a small cold aside from the narrator that Lebeziatnikov ‘remembered all this’ afterwards.

annotations.quote: Am I to get married simply for the sake of the furniture?
annotations.note: The funniest line Luzhin has been given, and he has no idea it is funny. The forfeited deposit hurts him in the same place as the loss of Dounia; in his ledger they are entries of one kind.

annotations.quote: why on earth was I such a Jew? It was false economy!
annotations.note: An ugly idiom, and it should be named as one: a stock slur for stinginess that Dostoevsky's characters, and Dostoevsky, used without blinking, and that Garnett renders straight. Look past it and the reasoning is ugly in its own right. His mistake, as he sees it, was not meanness but meanness that failed to pay. He goes on to price the presents that would have made Dounia unable to refuse him.

annotations.quote: What for many years past he had feared more than anything was _being shown up_
annotations.note: The key to Luzhin. The radical press of the 1860s made a sport of exposure, naming officials and their swindles, and a provincial lawyer with things to hide had reason to dread it. So he courts the young progressives the way one pays protection, which is why he arrived at [[p2c5|Raskolnikov's bedside]] with a mouthful of their phrases.

annotations.quote: who attach themselves to the idea most in fashion only to vulgarise it and who caricature every cause they serve, however sincerely.
annotations.note: The narrator drops his mask and editorialises, which he rarely does this bluntly. But read the last two words. ‘However sincerely’ is a concession, and I would hold on to it.

annotations.quote: she was suffering and that was her asset, so to speak, her capital which she had a perfect right to dispose of.
annotations.note: Sonia's prostitution translated into political economy: suffering as ‘capital.’ It is grotesque, and yet Lebeziatnikov is the only lodger in the house who says he respects her. Compare [[p1c2|her father telling the same story]], where the act was a sacrifice nobody could bear to look at.

annotations.quote: I feel it strange myself how timid, chaste and modern she is with me!
annotations.note: ‘Modern’ makes no sense here, and I am fairly sure it is an old misprint for ‘modest’ that has travelled with this text; the Russian word means bashful. Read it that way and the sentence becomes touching in spite of its speaker. The girl he lectures on free love is shy with him, and it honestly puzzles him.

annotations.quote: much better than the work of a Raphael and a Pushkin, because it is more useful.
annotations.note: A real slogan of the day, barely exaggerated. The radical critic Pisarev and his followers argued in earnest that a pair of boots was worth more than Pushkin. Dostoevsky, who thought beauty was something people could not live without, simply swaps the boots for a cesspool.

annotations.quote: But some of the notes he left on the table.
annotations.note: A whole sentence for what is not put away. Dostoevsky seldom spends words on a tabletop without a reason, and I would keep an eye on this one.

annotations.quote: She felt it horribly indecorous, especially for _her_, to look at another person’s money.
annotations.note: The italic is Sonia's own shame speaking: a girl of her trade must not even be seen glancing at banknotes. So her eyes go from the notes to the eye-glass to the ring to his face, with nowhere safe to rest. It is a small, exact picture of someone who has learned to feel accused before anyone accuses her.

annotations.quote: Lebeziatnikov remembered all this and reflected upon it afterwards.
annotations.note: A sentence from the future, the sort a narrator uses about someone who will later be asked what he saw. Luzhin has been ‘preoccupied’ and rubbing his hands ever since Sonia left, and we are not told why.

links.why: Luzhin's first appearance, reciting the progressive phrases we now learn he picked up from Lebeziatnikov as insurance.
The ‘fateful interview’ he is brooding over this morning, and the reason Raskolnikov's name makes him grind his teeth.
Marmeladov already told us about Lebeziatnikov: the beating of Katerina Ivanovna, the borrowed books, the science that forbids compassion.

p5c2.essay:
Dostoevsky has a form all his own, the scandal scene: fill a small room with people who should never share one, add drink and wounded pride, and wait. This is the fullest one yet, and what impresses me is how carefully he explains the fuse before lighting it. The opening paragraph is almost an essay on ‘poor man's pride,’ on why someone with no bread for tomorrow spends ten of her last twenty roubles on Lisbon wine and pancakes, and it refuses the easy answer. Luzhin, [[p5c1|a chapter ago]], called the dinner proof that she cannot be trusted with money. The narrator calls it ‘an irresistible nervous craving’ and then adds the sentence that matters: she ‘might have been killed by circumstance, but her spirit could not have been broken.’ That is said with respect.

Katerina Ivanovna is one of the great creations of the book because she is unbearable and right at once. She invents people's virtues and ‘quite genuinely’ believes in them; she has Luzhin down as her father's old guest on no evidence whatever; she waves a certificate that, read ‘en toutes lettres,’ demotes her father from colonel to major. She mocks her guests in a stage whisper while pressing food on them. And between the jokes she coughs blood into a handkerchief and shows it to Raskolnikov without a word. The laughter and the blood come out of the same mouth, and that is the chapter's whole method. Remember [[p1c2|Marmeladov in the tavern]], from whom the shawl dance and the certificate sounded like a drunkard's embroidery. Here is the paper itself, going greasy from hand to hand.

What the comedy keeps circling, quietly, is Sonia. The genteel ladies stayed away because of ‘that young person’; someone sends a crude valentine down the table to her; someone guffaws when her future is mentioned. The quarrel with the landlady about fathers and burgomeisters is farce, the best in the novel, but it only turns physical at the words ‘yellow ticket.’ Katerina Ivanovna will trade insults about her own birth all afternoon. She will not hear that one.

And Raskolnikov? He is nearly silent, eating out of politeness and watching Sonia ‘intently.’ After [[p4c4|what he told her last night]] it is fair to wonder what he is waiting for. He is the dinner's guest of honour and barely present at it. The chapter stops on an opened door.

annotations.quote: Even the poorest and most broken-spirited people are sometimes liable to these paroxysms of pride and vanity which take the form of an irresistible nervous craving.
annotations.note: The narrator tries ‘possibly,’ ‘perhaps’ and ‘very probable’ before settling here, on something closer to a symptom than a motive. This is how the book tends to explain people: by pressures, not reasons. It is worth setting beside Raskolnikov, another pauper who would rather go hungry than be looked down on.

annotations.quote: she would invent various circumstances to the credit of her new acquaintance and quite genuinely believe in their reality.
annotations.note: Her lies are generous, which sets them apart from everyone else's in this house. She has already promoted Luzhin to family friend and benefactor on the strength of one remark made in passing. A great deal of her afternoon is resting on him.

annotations.quote: She showed Raskolnikov the blood in silence
annotations.note: In the middle of a comic aria about owls and ribbons, seven words of plain fact. She does not comment and neither does he. Then she goes straight back to whispering jokes, and the jokes sound different.

annotations.quote: they found a gingerbread cock in his pocket; he was dead drunk, but he did not forget the children!
annotations.note: Her whole defence of the marriage in a single object. Whether it softens the picture of [[p2c7|the man carried in from the street]] or makes it worse, I cannot decide, and I doubt she can either. The clerk's leering ‘A cock?’ is the room's reply.

annotations.quote: an insult to Sonia meant more to Katerina Ivanovna than an insult to herself, her children, or her father.
annotations.note: This revises a first impression. In [[p1c2|Marmeladov's account]] it was the stepmother's taunt that sent Sonia out onto the street, and the stepmother who knelt at her feet all that evening. Everything fierce in Katerina Ivanovna today is that guilt turned outward as loyalty.

annotations.quote: a plate with two hearts pierced with an arrow, cut out of black bread.
annotations.note: A valentine carved from the cheapest loaf and passed down the table to the girl sitting beside Raskolnikov. It is a dirty joke about her trade and a jibe at him in one. Notice that Sonia is given no line of direct speech in this chapter; things are simply done at her.

annotations.quote: the cabman wanted him to kill, and Karl very much begged him not to kill
annotations.note: Garnett keeps the landlady's German word order, so the anecdote comes out as nonsense. But listen to its subject: a man begging not to be murdered, told for laughs, with Raskolnikov at the table saying nothing. Katerina Ivanovna then asks him to agree that the victim was an idiot for pleading.

annotations.quote: so that she really was almost the daughter of a colonel.
annotations.note: The narrator's driest joke. The document she carries as proof says major, in print, and she lets it go round the drunks all the same. ‘Almost’ is the word she lives in: almost a colonel's daughter, almost a governor's, almost in possession of a pension.

annotations.quote: since it was still uncertain whether her name was Amalia Ivanovna or Amalia Ludwigovna.
annotations.note: A patronymic is your father's name, so to dispute it is to say nobody knows who he was. ‘Ivanovna’ passes for Russian; ‘Ludwigovna’ pins her down as German. The novel itself seems unsure, since Marmeladov in [[p1c2]] called her Amalia Fyodorovna.

annotations.quote: He stood scanning the party with severe and vigilant eyes.
annotations.note: The guest she has been advertising all day arrives at the very second the landlady's cap is about to come off. ‘Vigilant’ is an odd word for a man walking in on a brawl. He is looking for someone.

links.why: Marmeladov's tavern monologue first described this room, this landlady, the shawl dance and the certificate now being passed round.
The same room two days earlier, at the deathbed, where Raskolnikov left the twenty roubles this dinner is spending.
Sonia's own description of Katerina Ivanovna, ‘like a child’ and expecting righteousness everywhere, reads as a forecast of this table.

p5c3.essay:
The trap closes, and the first thing to admire is how well it was built. Luzhin's long accusation is a piece of lawyer's work, and every detail we watched in [[p5c1]] has been turned into evidence. Sonia's shyness becomes ‘embarrassment,’ her three attempts to leave become trying ‘to make off,’ her tears become ingratitude, his ten roubles become the charity she repaid with theft. He insisted that Lebeziatnikov stay in the room, and now we see why: he cites him again and again. Even the landlady's reflexive ‘I knew she was the thief’ is pocketed at once as words ‘uttered before witnesses.’ Underneath the procedure sits the one argument that does the real work, ‘your social position and the habits associated with it.’ A girl with a yellow ticket is guilty in advance. ‘You reckoned on her meekness!’ Katerina Ivanovna shouts at him, and it is the most exact thing anyone says.

Then the note flies out of the pocket. Dostoevsky gives it a ‘parabola,’ a little arc of geometry in the middle of the screaming, and for a few paragraphs a reader who trusts Sonia has nothing to stand on except trust. That, I think, is the purpose of the interval. Katerina Ivanovna has no evidence either. She cries that she does not believe it ‘in the face of the obvious fact,’ rocking Sonia like a baby. For two chapters she has believed things that are untrue: her father's governorship, Luzhin's old friendship with the family. Here the same reckless faculty lands on the truth, and it is the only thing in the room that does. I find this the most moving stroke in the scene. Her fantasy and her loyalty turn out to be one organ.

Rescue comes from the direction nobody was looking, least of all the narrator, who two chapters ago filed Lebeziatnikov among the ‘dullards.’ The man with ‘something wrong with his eyes’ is the one who saw. His testimony is wonderful comedy. He will take an oath though it is ‘against my principles,’ he detours through Piderit and the ‘Positive Method,’ and his clinching proof is that he could not have had so many theories about the hundred roubles had there been no hundred roubles. But notice what the theories were. Watching Luzhin slip money into a girl's pocket, he could think only of kind explanations: a surprise, a test, modesty, the right hand not knowing (the Sermon on the Mount, half-remembered by an atheist). He was fooled because he is decent. Dostoevsky hates this man's ideas and still lets him be the one honest witness, and I trust the novelist more for it.

Lebeziatnikov supplies the fact; Raskolnikov supplies the motive, and this is the part I cannot read innocently. He has stood through the whole accusation ‘against the wall, with his arms crossed,’ silent even when Katerina Ivanovna begs him by name. Why so long? Partly he is waiting for the missing piece. But there is something of the observer in it too, a man watching an experiment run to its end. When he does speak he is superb: ‘clearly, calmly, exactly, firmly,’ reasoning from motive to act, naming his witnesses, offering to swear. It is the kind of reasoning [[p3c5|Porfiry]] has been practising on him, and he proves very good at it. The undiscovered murderer of two women becomes, for ten minutes, counsel for the defence of an innocent one, and the room believes him on the strength of his ‘stern face.’ Dostoevsky does not underline the irony. He has no need to.

One more thing sits in that speech. Explaining Luzhin's calculation, Raskolnikov says before the whole lodging-house that Sonia's ‘honour and happiness’ are ‘very precious’ to him. He offers it as a fact about what Luzhin supposed. It is also, plainly, a declaration.

The victory does nobody any good. Luzhin walks out threatening prosecution; a thrown glass hits the wrong person; the family is evicted before the table is cleared. Katerina Ivanovna runs off under [[p1c2|the green shawl]] to find ‘justice on earth,’ and the phrase is hard to bear because we have just seen what justice on earth nearly did. Sonia's own lesson comes in the narrator's quietest sentences: she had hoped that ‘care, gentleness and submissiveness’ would keep her safe. And Raskolnikov's parting thought is not pity. It is ‘we shall see what you'll say now,’ as though the afternoon had been staged as his rebuttal in [[p4c4|the argument they began last night]]. He goes to her with a point to make. He also has a promise to keep.

annotations.quote: I want to have a word with your stepdaughter, Sofya... Ivanovna, I think it is?
annotations.note: An hour ago, in his own room, he called her ‘my dear Sofya Semyonovna’ without hesitation. The fumbled patronymic is an act put on for the company: I hardly know this person. He gets it right again later in the chapter, once it suits him to be merciful.

annotations.quote: taking into consideration your social position and the habits associated with it
annotations.note: Here is the real evidence, tucked into a subordinate clause. The tallies, the pocket-book and the witnesses are scaffolding around a single assumption, that a prostitute steals. He is counting on the room to share it, and for a minute the room does.

annotations.quote: he stood against the wall, with his arms crossed, looking at her with glowing eyes.
annotations.note: Sonia looks to him for help and gets this. He does not move for another fifty paragraphs. I read the folded arms as a man making himself wait, but it is a hard posture to like, and Dostoevsky leaves it unexplained.

annotations.quote: a piece of paper flew out and describing a parabola in the air fell at Luzhin’s feet.
annotations.note: It is Katerina Ivanovna's own hand that produces the note, by forcing the search she was certain would clear Sonia. ‘Parabola’ is a schoolroom word, and it slows the moment to the one second in which every eye follows the same object. Luzhin then lifts it ‘in two fingers,’ as if it were soiled.

annotations.quote: she cried in the face of the obvious fact, swaying her to and fro in her arms like a baby
annotations.note: The narrator grants that the fact is ‘obvious’ and stands with her regardless. Her habit of believing what she needs to believe has looked like illness for two chapters. Here it is the only sound judgment in the room.

annotations.quote: Pyotr Petrovitch at any rate was at once moved to _compassion_.
annotations.note: The italics are a sneer, and an earned one. Having won, he forgives: no police, a moral for the girl, himself as the injured and generous party. He steals a glance at Raskolnikov immediately afterwards, which tells me whom the show of mercy is for.

annotations.quote: Now could I, could I, have all these ideas and reflections if I had not seen you put the hundred-rouble note in her pocket?
annotations.note: As logic this is ridiculous and as testimony it is entirely convincing, a nice joke on a man who worships the ‘positive method.’ What persuades the room is that every one of his guesses was charitable. A liar would have told a simpler story.

annotations.quote: for he has grounds for supposing that the honour and happiness of Sofya Semyonovna are very precious to me.
annotations.note: Offered as a point about Luzhin's motive, in the same level voice as the rest. But he has just told a room of drunk strangers, and her, what she is to him. I am not sure he hears himself say it.

annotations.quote: Yet till that moment she had fancied that she might escape misfortune by care, gentleness and submissiveness before everyone.
annotations.note: The narrator steps inside Sonia, which he has seldom done, and what he finds is a strategy that has just failed. She has been cleared, and it changes nothing about what she has learned: that she ‘could be wronged with impunity.’ Her tears come after the vindication, not before.

annotations.quote: Well, Sofya Semyonovna, we shall see what you’ll say now!
annotations.note: Not ‘poor girl.’ He leaves a wrecked room and three children huddled on a trunk with the air of a man who has just been handed an argument. It picks up where [[p4c4|their last conversation]] broke off, when he pressed her about what would become of the children and she could only answer that God would not let it be.

links.why: Go back to the interview in Lebeziatnikov's room and watch it again, this time with Luzhin's speech here as the script he was writing.
The letter in which Luzhin first insinuated that Raskolnikov's money had gone to Sonia, which Raskolnikov cites in his explanation.
The dinner where Raskolnikov told Luzhin he was ‘not worth the little finger’ of Sonia, the insult this scheme was meant to avenge.
Raskolnikov's parting line makes most sense beside the argument he and Sonia had in her room the night before.
